clue.text: Freely obtains seats

definitions.meaning: to bum a cigarette or a lift is to cadge it, getting it for nothing
the part of a person that meets the chair, and the part of the trousers that covers it

explanation.walkthrough: Four letters and no machinery: two meanings of one blunt word laid side by side. Everyman traditionally opens gently, which is worth knowing when the rest of the grid looks forbidding.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are colloquial: to bum something is to scrounge it for nothing, and a bum is the backside you sit down on.

clue.text: Piqued, as edges of four sofa beds bashed up

indicators.note: Anything bashed up has been knocked out of shape, and letters knocked out of shape do not come back in the order they went in.
The edges of a word are its outermost letters, so only the first and last of the number survive.

parts.note: the outside letters of FOUR, front and back
eight letters taken whole, straight off the page

explanation.walkthrough: The surface is a house move gone wrong, which is why 'edges' reads as furniture corners rather than as an instruction. Ten letters is a long anagram: pencil them out before guessing.
explanation.definitionFit: Piqued → BRASSED OFF: British slang for thoroughly fed up, the resentful irritation that being piqued names in politer company.

clue.text: Spreads out arms and a medal

indicators.note: Something out of true has left its proper arrangement, so these letters are no longer standing in the order printed.

parts.note: four letters straight into the mixture
the article counts too, so its A joins the six letters of the award

explanation.walkthrough: The surface shows a soldier laying out kit, and 'arms' is the word doing the misleading — weapons in the picture, limbs nowhere, letters all along.
explanation.definitionFit: Spreads → MARMALADES: marmalade is a preserve you spread on toast, so the plural names the class of thing rather than any one jar.

clue.text: Starting to crawl — and fall; our son's wobbly

indicators.note: Something wobbly will not stay put, and letters that will not stay put end up somewhere other than where they started.

parts.note: ten letters taken exactly as they stand, the semicolon ignored

explanation.walkthrough: A toddler learning to move is the picture and the meaning at once, which makes the anagram hard to see: every word of the surface belongs to the same scene.
explanation.definitionFit: Starting to crawl → ON ALL FOURS: a baby who has just begun crawling is down on hands and knees, which is the position the phrase names.

clue.text: Found in northern EU (Trondheim), something small and free of charge

definitions.text: something small and free of charge

indicators.note: What is found in a place was already sitting there, so the letters are lying untouched inside the words that follow.

parts.note: the run crosses three words in order: norther-N, then EU, then TRON-dheim

explanation.walkthrough: A city in brackets looks like a helpful aside and is really where half the letters live. Norway is not in the EU, so the geography is doing nothing but hiding.
explanation.definitionFit: something small and free of charge → NEUTRON: the uncharged particle in an atomic nucleus, so 'free of charge' means electrically neutral rather than costing nothing.

clue.text: Chopped sage and piece of lardo: an Italian dish

indicators.note: Chopping food cuts it up and mixes it about, and letters treated that way come back rearranged.

parts.note: the herb hands over all four of its letters

indicators.note: A piece is a fragment rather than the whole, so the cured pork surrenders just its opening letter.

parts.note: the opening letter of the italicised Italian word
the article looks as though it belongs to the definition, and is really two more letters of fodder

explanation.walkthrough: The colon invites you to read everything after it as the meaning, which is exactly where the last two letters of the mixture are hiding. Italics in a clue usually flag a foreign word.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian dish → LASAGNE: definition by example, since one named baked pasta stands in for the whole national menu.

clue.text: Help following mishaps if it's dark and it's stormy

definitions.note: 'Help' is a mass noun where the answer is plural: the setter names what the boxes contain rather than counting the boxes, which is how kit is normally spoken of.

indicators.note: A storm throws everything about, and letters caught in one come down in a different order from the one they went up in.

parts.note: nine letters, the apostrophe ignored as punctuation always is
the 'and' only joins the two phrases; the three letters beside it go into the mixture

explanation.walkthrough: 'It was a dark and stormy night' is the joke, and it is also the whole of the fodder — a quotation is a good hiding place because you read it as one lump.
explanation.definitionFit: Help following mishaps → FIRST-AID KITS: the packed boxes of dressings and antiseptic kept ready for the small accidents that need treating on the spot.

clue.text: Represented initially: Uranian fleet overhead, supposedly?

definitions.note: A semi-&lit: the four words after the colon both describe the answer and give up their opening letters, while 'Represented initially' is only the instruction to take them.

indicators.note: To represent something initially is to stand for it by its opening letters, which is the job the words after the colon are given.

parts.note: the first letter of each of the four words, in the order written

explanation.walkthrough: Uranian means of the planet Uranus, not of any alien, so the surface plants astronomy where the initials plant a sighting. A sceptical adverb is often the setter winking at you.
explanation.definitionFit: Uranian fleet overhead, supposedly? → UFOS: an unidentified flying object is by definition only supposed to be a craft, which is what the question mark concedes.

clue.text: Blonde perhaps going after small band

indicators.note: What goes after something trails behind it, so the hair colour is written second and the abbreviation leads.

parts.note: S is the size on a clothing label
ash blonde is one shade of fair hair, and 'perhaps' is what flags a single example

explanation.walkthrough: 'Perhaps' almost always means an example is standing in for its category, and here it works backwards: the category is in the clue and the example is in the grid.
explanation.definitionFit: band → SASH: a sash is the broad strip of cloth worn across the chest or round the waist, so 'band' is the plain physical sense of the word.

clue.text: After starters of awfully creamy rissoles, Everyman's beginning to see a bit of a spread?

indicators.note: Something placed after the rest arrives behind it, so the letter taken second sits at the back of the build.
A word's beginning is its opening character, so the setter's pen name gives up one letter and keeps the rest.
A starter is what comes first at table, and taken of words it asks for the letter each one starts with.

parts.note: the first letter of each of the three words, in order
the setter signs his puzzles Everyman, and here he is reduced to his initial

explanation.walkthrough: A setter writing himself into his own clue is a standing convention, and it nearly always means letters rather than a person. A spread here is an estate, not a buffet.
explanation.definitionFit: a bit of a spread → ACRE: one measured parcel of a large holding, 'spread' being the estate agent's word for a stretch of land.

clue.text: Having made alterations to some rugs where visitors sleep

indicators.note: To alter something is to change how it is put together, so these letters will not be staying in the arrangement handed to them.

parts.note: the three words hand over all ten letters just as they stand

explanation.walkthrough: The surface pictures a house being redecorated, which is why 'rugs' reads as furnishing rather than as raw material. Watch for 'to' and 'some': small words are fodder as often as they are filler.
explanation.definitionFit: where visitors sleep → GUEST ROOMS: the spare bedrooms a household keeps made up for people staying the night, named straight from who uses them.

clue.text: Subordinate to assist with con

parts.note: to second a motion is to back it, so seconding and assisting are the same act
a fiddle is a swindle, which is what a con is

explanation.walkthrough: Neither half of the wordplay is a musical word, yet both halves land in an orchestra — that collision is the whole joke, and it is why the surface reads as prison slang.
explanation.definitionFit: Subordinate → SECOND FIDDLE: to play second fiddle is to take the supporting part behind someone else, from the orchestral desk that never carries the tune.

clue.text: Reluctance to having your part in something noticed?

definitions.text: Reluctance to having your part in something noticed?

parts.note: the surface offers your share in some piece of business; the setter means an actor's role in a play
under lights, being noticed is the entire job, and dreading it is what locks a performer up

explanation.walkthrough: There is no wordplay to find — the clue is one picture read two ways. 'A part in something' sounds like blame until you hear it as a role, and then the whole sentence changes profession.
explanation.definitionFit: The clue defines the condition outright: a performer's dread is precisely a horror of being watched playing a role in front of an audience.

clue.text: Three-card trick seen on film in S American capital

indicators.note: In a down entry what sits on something else is written above it, so the card game goes in first and the recording underneath.

parts.note: three-card monte is the street swindle with two losing cards and one winner
a video is a film in its recorded form

explanation.walkthrough: Both halves are worth banking: monte is the crossword word for a card sharp's game, and 'film' points at the medium far more often than at the cinema.
explanation.definitionFit: S American capital → MONTEVIDEO: definition by example, Uruguay's capital standing for the general description, with S the usual shorthand for South.

clue.text: Spooner tells us: Franklin's elevated item for service

indicators.note: The Reverend Spooner swapped the opening sounds of two words, so anything he tells us is that phrase with its first sounds traded.

parts.note: Benjamin Franklin is Ben, and Spooner takes his B away and hands him a T
elevated means tall, and it collects the B that Ben's gave up

explanation.walkthrough: Say 'Ben's tall' and then trade the two opening sounds; the result runs together into the answer. A surname alone is often a first name in disguise.
explanation.definitionFit: item for service → TENNIS BALL: the ball is what a player serves to open a point, so 'service' is the racket-sport term rather than a favour or a church.

clue.text: Coerce fierce type to accept love

indicators.note: To accept a thing is to take it in and keep it there, so the beast opens up and the letter goes inside rather than alongside.

parts.note: a dragon is the standing example of a fierce creature
love is nothing on a tennis scoreboard, and nothing is written O

explanation.walkthrough: Love for O is one of the first conventions to learn: it turns up wherever a clue needs a single round letter. Read 'fierce type' as a person and you will never find it.
explanation.definitionFit: Coerce → DRAGOON: to dragoon someone is to force them into a course of action, from the mounted troops once billeted on civilians to compel obedience.

clue.text: Poised, aquiver, before House's final instalment

indicators.note: Anything aquiver is shaking, and letters shaken about settle in a different arrangement.
What comes before something is written in front of it, so the shaken letters lead and the single one closes.

parts.note: six letters into the mixture, taken as printed

indicators.note: The final part of a word is its last character, so the television title gives up only the letter it ends on.

parts.note: the last letter of the italicised title

explanation.walkthrough: 'Poised' and 'aquiver' contradict each other, and that jar is the signal: the first word is material and the second is the instruction. Italics mark the programme title.
explanation.definitionFit: instalment → EPISODE: a serial is issued one episode at a time, so each broadcast really is an instalment of the longer story.

clue.text: Loudly repulsed: tick on woodland creature in range

indicators.note: Something repulsed has been driven back the way it came, so the letters it points at are read from the far end.

parts.note: f is the musician's mark for forte, meaning played loudly

indicators.note: Read as 'on top of', it stacks the short word for a moment in front of the animal before the pair are turned round.

parts.note: a tick and a mo are both a moment — 'hang on half a tick'
deer are the standing inhabitants of a wood

explanation.walkthrough: The single letter is the hard part: f for forte is a musical direction, not an abbreviation of anything English, and it turns up whenever a clue says loudly or softly.
explanation.definitionFit: range → FREEDOM: range in the sense of scope or latitude, the room a person is allowed to move or act in, rather than a distance or a stove.

clue.text: Member of a family who may have performed many hits

definitions.text: Member of a family who may have performed many hits

parts.note: the surface offers an ordinary relative; the family the setter means is a crime syndicate
not chart-toppers but contract killings, which is that family's line of work

explanation.walkthrough: No letters to assemble — the clue turns entirely on two senses of 'hit'. When a surface mentions music and family together, crosswords are nearly always pointing at organised crime.
explanation.definitionFit: Read straight it is a relative with a pop career; read the setter's way it is a sworn member of the Sicilian mob, and hits are killings.

clue.text: Filming evidently proving problematic? Have a break

definitions.meaning: a director calling for the tenth attempt at one shot is having a bad morning
the same words as an instruction to the crew: stop for ten minutes

explanation.walkthrough: Both readings live in the same film studio, which is what makes the split hard to see: one counts attempts and the other counts minutes.
explanation.definitionFit: One sense numbers the attempts at a shot, the other is the call for ten minutes off — the same phrase doing studio duty twice over.

clue.text: Smaller around North, and higher pitched

indicators.note: To go around a thing is to enclose it, so the compass point ends up inside the other word rather than beside it.

parts.note: smaller in the comparative is tinier
N is the map abbreviation for north

explanation.walkthrough: The two words differ by a single letter, so the insertion is nearly invisible; comparative definitions like this one are a good check, because both clue and answer must end -er.
explanation.definitionFit: higher pitched → TINNIER: a tinny sound is thin and metallic, as if struck on a sheet of tin, and thin sounds sit high.

clue.text: To have and to hold?

definitions.note: Neither half is plural on its own: 'to have' is one verb in that form and 'to hold' is another, and it takes the pair of them to earn the final S.
definitions.meaning: the opening words of the marriage vow, and grammatically a verb in its bare to-form
the phrase that completes the vow, and a second verb in exactly the same form

explanation.walkthrough: The vow is so familiar that you read it as a promise rather than as grammar, which is the whole trick. Ask what kind of word each half is and the answer arrives at once.
explanation.definitionFit: Each half is a verb in its to-form, the dictionary form a grammarian names with this word, and two of them together account for the plural.

clue.text: Region better ventilated, did you say?

indicators.note: Asking whether you said it hands the clue to the ear, so what counts is the sound of the word and not its spelling.

parts.note: a better ventilated room is airier, and airier spoken aloud is what you write in the grid

explanation.walkthrough: Comparatives make good soundalikes because the -er ending is swallowed in speech. Four squares and a question mark at the end of the clue is usually a sound clue.
explanation.definitionFit: Region → AREA: a plain synonym, both naming a stretch of ground taken as a whole, though only one of them also covers a field of study.

clue.text: Drink bouzoukist's drunk?

indicators.note: What has been drunk has been swallowed, and something swallowed is now inside — which is where the letters are sitting.

parts.note: the drink's name is buried whole inside the word for the player of the instrument

explanation.walkthrough: A bouzouki is the Greek long-necked lute, so the surface and the answer share a country — which is exactly why you read the word as scenery instead of searching it.
explanation.definitionFit: Drink → OUZO: definition by example, Greece's aniseed spirit standing in for the general word, which is why no nationality is spelt out.

clue.text: Singer following multi-voice song in competition

indicators.note: What follows something comes along behind it, so the bird is written after the song and not in front of it.

parts.note: a round is a song sung in overlapping parts, like Frere Jacques
the robin is the garden bird that sings through the winter

explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' with a capital could be a name, a sewing machine or a bird, and only the crossing letters decide. Music holds the surface together while the meaning is a sports fixture list.
explanation.definitionFit: competition → ROUND ROBIN: the tournament format in which every entrant plays every other, so the phrase names a way of running a contest.

clue.text: Plan in E End: hole up in this location

indicators.note: East End speech leaves the aitch at the front of a word unsounded, so both words here lose theirs.

parts.note: to hole up somewhere is to hide there
this location is simply here
stripped of their aitches the two words run together into 'ide 'ere, which is what you say and not what you write

explanation.walkthrough: A dropped aitch is worth remembering: Cockney, E End or Bow Bells in a clue nearly always means an H has gone missing from the front of a word.
explanation.definitionFit: Plan → IDEA: the everyday sense in which you have an idea for how to proceed, which is a plan in embryo rather than a mere thought.

clue.text: Legitimate position of chess player's hand

definitions.meaning: describes an arrangement that is open and honest, with nothing going on out of sight
taken literally, the hand hovering over the pieces is exactly where the phrase puts it

explanation.walkthrough: The phrase comes from card play, where hands kept in sight cannot swap a card underneath the table; chess borrows the same picture without meaning anything by it.
explanation.definitionFit: Legitimate → ABOVE BOARD: from card tables, where a visible hand cannot cheat, and a chess player's really does hover over the board.

clue.text: Kitty to circle back

indicators.note: Coming back means retracing the way you came, so an across answer's letters are read from the far end to the near one.

parts.note: a loop is a circle drawn in a length of line or rope

explanation.walkthrough: Read 'circle' as a verb and there is nothing to find; read it as a shape and four letters arrive ready to turn. Short reversals are the ones most often missed.
explanation.definitionFit: Kitty → POOL: the shared fund everyone pays into and the winner takes, which is what a kitty is at a card table or in an office sweepstake.
